Remove rare, poorly genotyped or redundant SNPs

Source: R/filter.R
filter_snps.Rd

Most analyses of population structure work best on a cleaned-up set of SNPs. filter_snps() applies up to three filters, in this order, and records how many SNPs remain after each one (see summary.snpscape()).

Usage

filter_snps(
  x,
  min_maf = 0.01,
  max_missing = 0.05,
  prune_ld = FALSE,
  ld_r2 = 0.2,
  ld_window = 50
)

Arguments

x

A snpscape object.

min_maf

Minimum minor allele frequency, between 0 and 0.5.

max_missing

Maximum proportion of people with a missing genotype.

prune_ld

Remove SNPs in strong linkage disequilibrium with a neighbour (TRUE or FALSE).

ld_r2

Maximum r² allowed between SNPs within a window when prune_ld = TRUE.

ld_window

Window size, in number of SNPs, for LD pruning.

Value

The filtered snpscape object.

Details

1. Minor allele frequency (min_maf)

The minor allele frequency (MAF) is the frequency of the less common of a SNP's two alleles. Most SNPs in the human genome are very rare: they are carried by only one or a handful of people. Rare SNPs say little about differences between populations, add noise, and (when nobody in the data carries the minor allele at all) cannot be analysed by PCA. Removing SNPs with a MAF below 1% (min_maf = 0.01) is a common choice.

MAF is calculated from the people currently in the data, so if you later remove populations with keep_pops(), some SNPs may become rare again.

2. Missing genotypes (max_missing)

SNPs for which genotypes are unknown for many people are removed. The 1000 Genomes high-coverage data have very few missing genotypes, so this filter rarely removes anything, but it is good practice.

3. Linkage disequilibrium pruning (prune_ld)

Nearby SNPs tend to be inherited together, because chromosomes are passed down in long chunks that are only occasionally broken up by recombination. This correlation between neighbouring SNPs is called linkage disequilibrium (LD). In a small region, many SNPs may be strongly correlated and so carry almost the same information. Methods like PCA and admixture analysis assume each SNP is independent evidence; a block of correlated SNPs effectively gets counted many times and can dominate the result.

LD pruning keeps a set of SNPs that are only weakly correlated with each other. It moves a window of ld_window SNPs along the region and, within each window, whenever two SNPs have a squared correlation (r²) above ld_r2, removes the one with the lower minor allele frequency. This is a simplified version of the widely used --indep-pairwise method of the PLINK program.

Pruning is off by default. Turn it on (prune_ld = TRUE) for PCA and admixture analysis. Leave it off when you are interested in LD itself or in particular SNPs.

Examples

lct <- example_lct |>
  filter_snps(min_maf = 0.05, prune_ld = TRUE)
summary(lct)
